paragraphs: Combining different kinds of information is difficult because relationships can mean different things in different settings. A single shared representation may overlook those differences. Cooperation of Experts addresses this problem by organizing multiple information types into a heterogeneous multiplex network: a unified structure that can retain different kinds of objects and connections.

Within this structure, separate encoders serve as experts for particular semantic spaces. Each learns the relational patterns appropriate to its own domain. The experts then cooperate through a large-margin mechanism and a dedicated optimization strategy. This cooperation is intended to extract complementary information and improve robustness while retaining the value of specialized representations.

The paper provides theoretical analyses supporting the framework’s feasibility and stability, alongside experiments reporting superior performance across diverse benchmarks. These contributions address two separate questions: whether the proposed cooperation is mathematically well supported, and whether it helps on evaluated data. The stated findings support combining specialized relational learning with coordinated information fusion.
icml-2025-cooperation-of-experts-fusing-.tldr: Cooperation of Experts combines specialized network encoders through a large-margin mechanism to fuse heterogeneous information.

paragraphs: Graph fairness learning aims to make predictions that are unbiased with respect to sensitive attributes. Many existing approaches assume that training and test data follow the same distribution. DANCE addresses the harder situation in which that distribution changes, combining simulated shifts with objectives intended to preserve fairness.

The method creates challenging virtual data in two places: the graph itself and the model’s hidden representation space. In hidden space, an unbiased Mixup procedure prioritizes minority groups to address sensitive-attribute imbalance. In graph space, fairness-aware adversarial learning emphasizes difficult examples to improve robustness. These two forms of expansion expose the model to variation beyond its original training data.

DANCE also aligns domains using a group-based objective that prioritizes negative pairs sharing sensitive labels. A further disentanglement objective reduces correlation between sensitive attributes and representations used for the prediction target. The reported experiments demonstrate the method’s superior effectiveness. Together, the components target distribution changes, group imbalance, and sensitive information in representations within one learning framework.
icml-2025-dance-dual-unbiased-expansion-.tldr: DANCE combines virtual graph data, group-aware alignment, and representation disentanglement to improve graph fairness under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Pretrained interatomic potentials predict properties needed for simulations of materials, but demanding tasks can still require fine-tuning. For models built around rotation-equivariant graph neural networks, adaptation must preserve how predictions respond to rotations. The paper argues that conventional parameter-efficient methods break this symmetry when applied to these networks.

ELoRA introduces low-rank adaptation specifically structured for SO(3)-equivariant networks. Its weight updates use a path-dependent decomposition that preserves the network’s rotational symmetry during fine-tuning. The authors prove this preservation property. The low-rank structure also improves data efficiency, making the adaptation method relevant to both physical consistency and the amount of data required.

On the rMD17 organic dataset, ELoRA reports improvements of 25.5% in energy prediction accuracy and 23.7% in force prediction accuracy relative to full-parameter fine-tuning. Across ten inorganic datasets, the corresponding average improvements are 12.3% and 14.4%. These experimental results show that, in the evaluated settings, preserving symmetry through carefully structured updates can accompany better predictive accuracy than updating every parameter.
icml-2025-elora-low-rank-adaptation-for-.tldr: ELoRA preserves rotational symmetry during low-rank fine-tuning of interatomic models and improves energy and force predictions in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Event-customized image generation asks a model to preserve the actions, poses, relationships, and interactions in a reference scene while changing its entities. This extends customization beyond appearance or simple interactions between two participants. The paper formulates the task using a single reference image, making the whole scene’s event the object of customization.

Its proposed method, FreeEvent, adds two paths to diffusion denoising without requiring training. The entity-switching path uses cross-attention guidance and regulation to generate the requested entities. The event-transfer path injects spatial features and self-attention maps from the reference image into the target generation. These paths address who appears in the image and how the scene’s participants relate to one another.

The authors also collect SWiG-Event and Real-Event as evaluation benchmarks. Experiments and ablations support FreeEvent’s effectiveness on the proposed task. The contribution therefore includes both a generation method and resources for evaluating a broader customization objective: transferring a complex event from one reference while allowing its participating entities to change.
icml-2025-event-customized-image-generat.tldr: FreeEvent transfers a reference image’s complex actions and relationships to new entities through training-free diffusion guidance.

paragraphs: Prompt design usually emphasizes clear instructions and understandable demonstrations. This paper reports a surprising alternative: selectively pruning random demonstrations can produce apparently incoherent text that improves model performance. Across the reported evaluations, these prompts match or exceed leading automatic prompt-optimization methods, with gains observed across models regardless of alignment.

Finding useful pruning patterns is itself difficult. The authors report that existing attribution and prompt-compression approaches do not reliably solve this problem. They introduce PromptQuine, an evolutionary search framework that discovers and refines pruning strategies using little data. Its search draws only on tokens already present in the context, making the existing prompt material the resource from which new prompts evolve.

The evaluation covers classification, multiple-choice answering, generation, and mathematical reasoning across language models, with reported runtime efficiency. These findings suggest that human-readable coherence is not a reliable guide to which demonstrations will help in-context learning. The paper positions this result as motivation for mechanistic investigations and more open-ended prompt search.
icml-2025-evolving-prompts-in-context-an.tldr: PromptQuine evolves pruned, seemingly incoherent demonstrations that perform strongly across the paper’s language-model evaluations.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein barycenter represents several probability distributions by minimizing their total Wasserstein distance to a central distribution. That aggregate objective can leave an underrepresented distribution far from the result. The paper proposes the Wasserstein Ball Center to address this issue by focusing on the largest distance to any input distribution.

The resulting objective seeks a center with the smallest possible enclosing radius in Wasserstein distance. This minmax formulation gives the most distant input a direct role in determining the solution. For fixed support, the authors show that the problem becomes a large linear program, with a structure different from the previously studied barycenter formulation.

The algorithm exploits properties of the associated normal equation to accelerate an interior-point method by O(min(N²m, Nm², m⁴)), where N counts distributions and m is support size. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate computational efficiency and improved fairness for the input distributions. Here, the fairness motivation is specifically tied to reducing how far any represented distribution can lie from the center.
icml-2025-finding-wasserstein-ball-cente.tldr: The Wasserstein Ball Center minimizes the worst distance to input distributions, with an efficient fixed-support algorithm and fairness-motivated results.

paragraphs: Freeze-Omni connects speech input and output to a text-based language model while keeping that model’s parameters fixed throughout training. The aim is to make the backbone’s existing capabilities available through spoken conversation, without needing to update the language model itself when learning the speech interface.

This architecture separates the addition of speech modalities from changes to the textual backbone. The authors report that Freeze-Omni maintains the backbone’s level of intelligence in speech while providing low-latency spoken responses. Keeping the language model frozen also addresses the catastrophic-forgetting concern that can arise when adapting it with limited training data and resources.

The paper additionally develops multitask training for duplex dialogue, supporting a more natural style of user-agent speech interaction. The contribution combines an architectural choice about which parameters remain fixed with a training approach for conversational behavior. Its stated significance is that responsive speech-to-speech dialogue can be built around a frozen language model while retaining the capabilities already available through text.
icml-2025-freeze-omni-a-smart-and-low-la.tldr: Freeze-Omni adds low-latency speech input, speech output, and duplex dialogue to a language model whose parameters remain frozen.

paragraphs: A model that can produce a solution still needs to judge whether criticism of that solution is valid. Accepting every correction can overturn a correct answer, while rejecting every correction prevents useful revision. This paper studies whether self-play can improve that judgment without supervision from humans or stronger models.

The proposed Critic-Discernment Game begins with a prover solving a problem. It then receives critiques that may be helpful or deliberately misleading. The prover’s objective depends on the situation: preserve a correct answer under misleading criticism, and repair an incorrect answer when the feedback is constructive. The training game therefore rewards selective responsiveness to criticism.

Experiments examine mathematical reasoning, identification of errors within reasoning steps, self-correction, and long reasoning chains. The authors report that CDG training can substantially improve well-aligned models’ comprehension of their own reasoning processes. The stated finding concerns this evaluated class of models and supports self-play as a way to improve how they assess and revise reasoning.
icml-2025-improving-rationality-in-the-r.tldr: The Critic-Discernment Game uses self-play to help well-aligned models accept useful critiques and resist misleading ones.

paragraphs: Image-restoration bridge models define a diffusion process that takes a degraded image toward a clear one. Existing approaches typically train a separate bridge for each degradation type, which creates substantial computational cost. IRBridge investigates how to reuse pretrained generative models within these restoration processes.

The central obstacle is a mismatch between starting points. Standard generative diffusion begins from pure noise, whereas restoration begins from an image that already contains degraded visual information. Consequently, the states encountered along the two processes have different distributions. The authors derive a transition equation connecting diffusion processes that share the same endpoint distribution, providing the basis for transferring generative knowledge between them.

IRBridge uses this connection to incorporate generative models directly into restoration bridges, removing the stated need to train each bridge from scratch. Experiments across six restoration tasks report improved robustness and generalization through efficient integration of pretrained generative priors. The approach matters because it provides a principled connection between existing image generators and restoration processes with different starting conditions.
icml-2025-irbridge-solving-image-restora.tldr: IRBridge connects diffusion processes with a shared endpoint so pretrained image generators can be reused in image-restoration bridges.

paragraphs: Time-series signals contain information that changes over time, but connecting those signals to natural-language questions is challenging. This paper introduces Time-Series Question Answering as a task for studying that connection. It also releases EngineMT-QA, a large-scale dataset spanning multiple tasks and interactions between temporal signals and language.

The proposed Instruct Time Transformer, or ITFormer, connects time-series encoders to a frozen large language model. Its role is to extract, align, and fuse temporal and textual features so that the language model can answer questions involving time-series information. Keeping the language model frozen makes the connecting framework central to learning the relationship between the modalities.

The authors report a strong improvement in question-answering accuracy over strong baselines while adding fewer than 1% trainable parameters. This result links predictive improvements with a small trainable extension. The dataset and framework together provide a way to investigate interactive language-based access to temporal data, beyond treating time-series processing and natural-language answering as separate tasks.
icml-2025-itformer-bridging-time-series-.tldr: ITFormer links time-series encoders to frozen language models for question answering, supported by the new EngineMT-QA dataset.

paragraphs: Motion transfer animates an object from a source image using poses from a driving video. Large differences between source and driving poses are difficult for existing unsupervised methods to model. This paper addresses that difficulty by generating intermediate images, turning a large displacement into a sequence of smaller motion changes.

The method can interpolate at different points between the source and driving images. A selector chooses an interpolated image for the downstream task, reducing the remaining motion difference that must be handled. Because real images are unavailable as labels for these intermediate states, the authors introduce bidirectional training and constraints on the selected image. Additional constraint losses use a pretrained Vision Transformer to encourage image quality.

The experiments support the central premise: transferring motion across the smaller gap between an interpolated image and a driving image is easier than handling the original large gap. The method also reports significant improvements in motion-related metrics over existing state-of-the-art approaches. Interpolation thus serves as an intermediate computational step for making difficult motion transfer more manageable.
icml-2025-large-displacement-motion-tran.tldr: The method improves large-displacement motion transfer by learning intermediate images that reduce the motion gap to the driving pose.

paragraphs: Multiple views can help a reinforcement-learning agent perceive its environment, but they also introduce redundant or distracting information. Some views may be missing altogether. Multi-view Fusion State for Control, or MFSC, seeks a compact representation that combines useful information across observations while retaining what matters for control.

MFSC incorporates bisimulation metric learning into multi-view reinforcement learning to guide task-relevant representations. It also adds an auxiliary task that masks information across views and reconstructs latent representations. A mask token explicitly represents missing views. This training design uses information shared across observations to improve the representation’s robustness when not every view is available.

The reported experiments show better performance than existing approaches on multi-view reinforcement-learning tasks. MFSC also maintains high performance in evaluated scenarios involving interference or absent views. These findings support the value of jointly learning which information matters for control and how views can compensate for one another. The contribution concerns useful fusion under imperfect observation conditions, as well as ordinary multi-view performance.
icml-2025-learning-fused-state-represent.tldr: MFSC learns control-relevant representations from multiple views and uses masked reconstruction to improve robustness to distractions and missing observations.

paragraphs: Latent-space memory stores past information in a language model’s hidden representations, offering a way to extend access beyond its ordinary context window. Retaining distant information remains difficult, however. The paper describes MemoryLLM as effective for sequences up to 16,000 tokens but struggling to retain knowledge beyond 20,000, despite its billion-parameter memory pool.

M+ extends MemoryLLM with a long-term memory mechanism and a retriever trained alongside it. During text generation, the retriever dynamically brings back relevant stored information. This couples memory storage with a learned process for deciding which past information should be available when producing the current response.

The evaluation covers long-context understanding and knowledge-retention tasks. M+ significantly outperforms MemoryLLM and recent strong baselines in the reported experiments, extending retention from below 20,000 to above 160,000 tokens with similar GPU memory overhead. The result shows that the added storage-and-retrieval mechanism can substantially lengthen usable memory in the tested setting without a comparable increase in GPU memory requirements.
icml-2025-m-extending-memoryllm-with-sca.tldr: M+ adds long-term memory and a co-trained retriever to MemoryLLM, extending reported knowledge retention beyond 160,000 tokens.

paragraphs: Audio-language models commonly require large collections of paired recordings and text, making data collection and training expensive. MATS investigates how to give a language model audio comprehension using text-only supervision. Its approach relies on an already pretrained audio-language alignment model, such as CLAP, rather than learning that alignment from scratch.

The training strategy projects the alignment model’s shared audio-language representation into the language model’s representation space. This allows MATS training to use text without audio examples. However, audio and language embeddings within CLAP still differ. The proposed Santa mechanism addresses that gap by mapping audio embeddings into CLAP’s language-embedding space while preserving essential information from the incoming audio.

Experiments report competitive performance against recent audio-language models trained on large paired datasets. The result concerns text-only training of MATS using pretrained alignment capabilities; those capabilities are an essential part of the approach. The work shows how an existing connection between sound and text can support multiple audio tasks while reducing the need for paired audio-language supervision during this training stage.
icml-2025-mats-an-audio-language-model-u.tldr: MATS uses pretrained audio-text alignment and text-only training to achieve competitive performance on multiple audio tasks.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies can learn strong robotic behavior from demonstrations, but generating an action through repeated denoising takes time. That delay matters when a robot must respond quickly or has limited computing resources. One-Step Diffusion Policy, or OneDP, compresses a pretrained diffusion policy into an action generator that uses a single step.

The distillation process aims to keep the new generator close to the original policy’s distribution. It does so by minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence along the diffusion chain. The authors report convergence with an additional cost equivalent to 2%–10% of pretraining, connecting the speed improvement to a relatively small additional training investment.

Evaluation includes six simulation tasks and four real-world tasks designed by the authors using a Franka robot. OneDP reports state-of-the-art success rates alongside much faster inference, with action prediction frequency increasing from 1.5 Hz to 62 Hz. These results support the possibility of retaining strong task performance while substantially reducing action-generation delay, which is particularly relevant for dynamic and computationally constrained robotic operation.
icml-2025-one-step-diffusion-policy-fast.tldr: OneDP distills diffusion-based robot policies into single-step action generators, reporting strong success rates and substantially faster inference.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation while preserving the output distribution. Existing approaches commonly divide work between a drafting model and a verifying model. This paper generalizes that arrangement to a polybasic framework involving multiple models, using theoretical analysis to guide how their work should be coordinated.

The authors prove a theorem characterizing optimal inference time for multi-model speculative decoding. Their analysis connects model capabilities, accepted token lengths, and total computational cost. These quantities determine whether extra speculative work is worthwhile. The framework can operate on its own or be integrated with existing speculative techniques, providing multiple routes for applying the analysis.

Experiments report speedups of 3.31×–4.01× for LLaMA2-Chat 7B, up to 3.87× for LLaMA3-8B, up to 4.43× for Vicuna-7B, and up to 3.85× for Qwen2-7B. The original output distribution is preserved. The findings support multi-model speculation as a practical acceleration strategy, with the theory clarifying how acceptance behavior and computation interact rather than assuming that adding models automatically improves speed.
icml-2025-polybasic-speculative-decoding.tldr: Polybasic speculative decoding uses theory to coordinate multiple models for faster generation while preserving the original output distribution.

paragraphs: Generating a polymer conformation means constructing an atomic-level arrangement of its structure. Methods developed for small molecules and proteins struggle with polymers’ distinct structural characteristics, while scarce datasets make progress harder. PolyConf addresses both issues with a generation method designed for polymers and a new evaluation resource.

The method divides a polymer into the local conformations of its repeating units. An autoregressive model generates these local structures, and a diffusion model generates their orientation transformations so they can be assembled into a complete conformation. This hierarchy separates the task of forming individual units from the task of arranging them within the larger polymer.

The authors also introduce a benchmark containing polymer conformations derived from molecular dynamics simulations. Their comprehensive evaluation reports that PolyConf consistently outperforms existing conformation-generation methods. The combined contribution is a structure-aware modeling approach and a dataset for comparing methods in an area with limited resources. The stated results support its use in advancing polymer modeling and simulation.
icml-2025-polyconf-unlocking-polymer-con.tldr: PolyConf generates polymer structures hierarchically by modeling repeating units and their orientations, supported by a new simulation-derived benchmark.

paragraphs: Density-ratio estimation measures how the probability density under one distribution compares with that under another. It supports applications including adaptation to covariate shift, causal inference, and independence testing. The paper addresses a trade-off: restrictive parametric models can introduce bias when misspecified, while conventional nonparametric methods struggle as the number of data dimensions grows.

The proposed estimator uses a projection-pursuit approximation. The approach works through projections to mitigate the difficulty of high-dimensional estimation while retaining flexibility in the density ratio being modeled. Its goal is to reduce the dimensional burden without relying on a rigid model form that may poorly match the data.

The authors establish consistency and a convergence rate for the estimator, providing theoretical support for its behavior as data increase. Experiments also report better performance than existing alternatives across several applications. These results combine an asymptotic statistical justification with empirical evidence that projection pursuit can offer a useful balance between model flexibility and the challenges of high-dimensional density-ratio estimation.
icml-2025-projection-pursuit-density-rat.tldr: Projection-pursuit density-ratio estimation addresses high-dimensional difficulty while retaining flexibility, with convergence guarantees and favorable experimental results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a principal can identify a desirable scoring rule through repeated interactions with an agent in an information-acquisition setting. The learning problem is viewed from the principal’s perspective: interaction provides the information needed to decide which rule to use. The central concern is how efficiently that decision can be made.

Two algorithms address different ways of controlling the learning process. OIAFC handles a fixed-confidence setting, where the desired reliability is specified. OIAFB handles a fixed-budget setting, where the available interaction budget is specified. This distinction separates a requirement on confidence from a requirement on how many interactions the procedure may use.

For OIAFC, the authors establish efficient sample-complexity bounds for obtaining the desired epsilon-delta scoring rule, including both instance-dependent and instance-independent forms. They also show that OIAFB matches OIAFC’s instance-independent performance bound and that the algorithms share the stated complexity across the two settings. The contribution is a theoretical account of efficient rule identification under these alternative resource requirements.
icml-2025-provably-efficient-algorithm-f.tldr: OIAFC and OIAFB provide theoretically efficient scoring-rule identification under fixed-confidence and fixed-budget interaction settings.

paragraphs: High-resolution images present multimodal language models with a large amount of visual information to process. Retrieval-Augmented Perception, or RAP, applies retrieval ideas to this challenge by selecting relevant image crops. The framework requires no training and combines the retrieved regions into information the model can use for its task.

Selecting a crop alone does not preserve its relationship to the full image. RAP therefore introduces a Spatial-Awareness Layout to retain spatial context when fusing crops. Its Retrieved-Exploration Search also adjusts how many regions to select, using model confidence and retrieval scores. This lets the amount of retrieved visual material respond to the task rather than remain fixed.

Experiments on high-resolution benchmarks report a 43% improvement on V* Bench and a 19% improvement on HR-Bench for LLaVA-v1.5-13B. These findings support retrieving relevant visual regions while preserving their layout as an effective way to improve perception in the evaluated setting. The method combines selection of image detail with control over how much detail is supplied.
icml-2025-retrieval-augmented-perception.tldr: RAP improves high-resolution image perception by dynamically retrieving relevant crops and preserving their spatial context without training.

paragraphs: Language models receive messages with different roles, including system instructions, user requests, and tool outputs. Reliable behavior requires distinguishing those roles. This paper examines whether fine-tuning teaches models that distinction or encourages them to recognize incidental patterns associated with particular roles in the training examples.

In controlled experiments focused on system and user tokens, the authors identify two shortcuts: using task type as a clue to role, and relying on proximity to the beginning of the text. Data augmentation partially reduces these behaviors, but the authors find that it generally leads to repeated patching. The underlying role distinction can remain entangled with superficial cues.

The proposed intervention strengthens invariant role-boundary signals through changes to token-level input encoding. In particular, modifying position IDs helps models distinguish roles more clearly and reduces shortcut reliance. The findings support investigating how role information is encoded, alongside which examples appear during training. The demonstrated improvement concerns clearer role learning, providing a mechanism-focused direction for more consistent behavior across multi-role inputs.
icml-2025-the-illusion-of-role-separatio.tldr: The paper identifies shortcuts in LLM role learning and reduces them by strengthening role-boundary cues through input encoding.

paragraphs: This paper investigates what changes inside a language model when fine-tuning substantially improves its performance. It constructs mathematical tasks where the pretrained model has meaningful room to improve, then identifies internal circuits at multiple training checkpoints. This setup examines learning beyond tasks the starting model already handles well.

The experiments find that circuit nodes remain highly similar before and after fine-tuning, while connections between those nodes change substantially. This contrasts with earlier findings of only small circuit additions. The result points to changes in internal connectivity as an important part of adaptation in these experiments, even when many participating components remain similar.

The authors use this observation to design circuit-aware LoRA, assigning adaptation ranks to layers according to changes in circuit edges. It achieves a reported average improvement of 2.46% over standard LoRA at comparable parameter sizes. The paper also explores combining subtask circuits to improve fine-tuning on compositional tasks. Together, these investigations connect circuit analysis to both an explanation of adaptation and a practical method for allocating adaptation capacity.
icml-2025-towards-understanding-fine-tun.tldr: Circuit analysis reveals substantial connection changes during fine-tuning and guides a LoRA variant that improves reported performance.

paragraphs: Choosing prices is difficult when a product or market has little historical data. This paper studies how observations from a related source domain can improve pricing in a target domain. It assumes covariate shift: the distributions of contextual variables may differ between domains, but their reward functions remain the same.

The proposed Transfer Learning for Dynamic Pricing algorithm uses previously collected source data to guide target-domain decisions. The authors establish a regret upper bound under a Lipschitz condition, which constrains how quickly the reward function can change. The guarantee therefore connects the usefulness of transfer to a defined relationship between domains and a smoothness requirement on rewards.

A matching minimax lower bound establishes the algorithm’s optimality in the analyzed setting. This bound also includes learning from target data alone as a special case. Numerical experiments report superiority over existing methods and support the approach’s practical relevance. The contribution combines a transfer-based pricing procedure with matching theoretical bounds, clarifying what performance is achievable under the stated assumptions.
icml-2025-transfer-learning-for-nonparam.tldr: TLDP transfers historical data into contextual pricing decisions with matching regret bounds under shared reward functions and covariate shift.

paragraphs: A calibrated model’s confidence should match how often its predictions are correct. This paper finds that prompt tuning in vision-language models can create a trade-off between calibration on base classes and new classes. Standard cross-entropy tuning can make new-class predictions overconfident by increasing divergence among textual label representations.

Regularization-based tuning produces a different problem: confidence stays similar while base-class accuracy improves, leaving the model underconfident on those classes. The authors introduce Dynamic Outlier Regularization to address both behaviors. DOR minimizes feature changes for novel textual labels sampled from a large vocabulary, directing regularization toward labels outside the base classes.

This choice aims to prevent increased textual divergence for new labels while relaxing constraints on base-class representations. Experiments show that DOR can improve calibration for both groups when applied to existing fine-tuning methods. The contribution links a confidence problem to changes in textual representations and proposes a targeted regularizer, rather than treating all labels as needing the same restrictions during adaptation.
icml-2025-understanding-and-mitigating-m.tldr: DOR regularizes novel textual labels to improve confidence calibration for both base and new classes after prompt tuning.

paragraphs: K-means is simple and efficient, but its results can depend on initial centroid choices, and ordinary Euclidean geometry can miss nonlinear structure in data. It can also struggle to produce balanced clusters. This paper develops a unified clustering framework that incorporates manifold learning to address these weaknesses.

The approach removes centroid calculation and uses a cluster indicator matrix to align manifold structures. That matrix represents cluster assignments within the learning process. The framework also extends beyond Euclidean distance by incorporating Gaussian-kernel, nearest-neighbor, and low-pass-filtering distances. These alternatives provide ways to account for relationships that ordinary straight-line distance may not capture in data that are not linearly separable.

A balancing regularizer further encourages balanced clustering results. The reported experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the overall methodology. Its contribution is to bring assignment information, nonlinear data structure, and cluster balance into one formulation. This changes both how relationships among data points are represented and how cluster assignments are encouraged, while retaining k-means as the starting point.
icml-2025-unified-k-means-clustering-wit.tldr: The framework combines centroid-free k-means, manifold-aware distances, and a balancing regularizer to improve clustering.
